summary.text: One of Portugal's oldest and best-known golf clubs, a short, tree-lined par 69 that overlooks Estoril and the sea.

setting.text: The course overlooks Estoril and the sea and winds through eucalyptus, mimosa and pine trees.
The club says it forces players to rely on accuracy rather than distance.
The championship course is a par 69 (34 out, 35 back) of 5,189 metres, according to the club.
Top100golfcourses calls it a rather hilly and rather short course, with tight fairways either side of the A5 motorway.
A reviewer on Golf by TourMiss describes crossing a bridge high above a major highway that splits the course.
There is also a nine-hole Blue Course, normally used by beginners.

history.text: The club says golf here began in 1929, when Fausto Figueiredo, who held the concession for the Estoril Casino and owned two hotels in the area, opened the first nine holes, designed by the Frenchman Jean Gassiat.
The club says the second nine holes, designed by the Scottish architect Philip Mackenzie Ross, opened in 1945 and the remaining holes were adapted.
The members' Clube de Golf do Estoril was founded in 1945 by a group of Portuguese players, who took over the lease of the course and clubhouse. The current clubhouse opened in 1948.
Top100golfcourses says Mackenzie Ross was a former design partner of Tom Simpson and also worked at other Portuguese courses in the 1930s.
The club's oldest trophy dates from 1938 and is named after Ricardo Espirito Santo Silva, first president of the Portuguese Golf Federation.
Top100golfcourses says Estoril, with Oporto, Miramar and Lisbon Sports Club, helped form the Portuguese Golf Federation in 1949.
Portugal's first golf professionals, Henrique Paulino, Joaquim Rodrigues and Carlos Aleixo, trained at the club.

In 1993 the course was changed to make way for the Lisbon-Estoril motorway, by the French architect Jean Jean. The old 9th disappeared, the 13th was reshaped, a new 151-metre par three was added between the 13th and 14th, the 16th was reconfigured and the holes were renumbered.

trivia.text: The club hosted the Portuguese Open for 20 editions, from its start in 1953 to 1987, according to Top100golfcourses.
The Open de Portugal winners at Estoril include Eric Brown (1953), Peter Alliss (1958), Max Faulkner (1968) and Robert Lee (1987).
Robert Lee's 1987 win was over 54 holes, on 195 (12 under par), one stroke ahead of Sam Torrance. It was the last Portuguese Open played at Estoril.
The club says it also hosted the International Amateur Championship for 63 years.
The club names Ballesteros, Montgomerie, Sam Torrance, Canizares, Gene Sarazen, Peter Alliss and Bernard Gallacher among the players who have competed there.
Top100golfcourses says a lack of length is largely down to having only two par fives.
Top100golfcourses quotes William fforde calling it 'full of history and not to be underestimated', a short, pretty, tree-lined course with narrow fairways and subtle, hard-to-find greens.
Top100golfcourses' Portugal ranking history lists Estoril as a debut entry in the 2020 Top 50.
A TourMiss reviewer said it is a course where golf is 'more akin to a game of chess' than a test of power, and that any miss from the fairway is likely to cost a bogey or worse.

local.text: Estoril is a seaside resort with a famous casino and beach, about 25 minutes by car from Lisbon.
The original 1929 course was meant as a leisure space for tourists and the foreign community living in Portugal.
